name: Hostile media effect
statement: Partisans on opposite sides of an issue read the same balanced news report and each side judges it slanted against them.
meaning: Two claims travel under one name and they are tested differently. The absolute version says each partisan group places the same coverage on the hostile side of a rating scale, so pro and anti readers land on opposite sides of the neutral midpoint. The relative version, named by Gunther, Christen, Liebhart and Chia, says only that the two groups differ in the predicted directions. Under the relative version both sides can agree that a story favours one camp while the camp it disfavours sees more slant, and that still counts. The relative test is the easier one to pass, and most of what is reported as a hostile media effect since 2001 is relative. The mechanism proposed for it is not media hostility. Gunther and Schmitt argue that a mass medium reaches an audience of strangers, and that partisans read content as hostile when they think about what it will do to those strangers.

origin.who: Robert P. Vallone, Lee Ross and Mark R. Lepper
origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: Their article ran in volume 49, issue 3, pages 577 to 585, and showed pro-Israeli and pro-Arab students the same network news coverage of the 1982 Beirut massacre, with each group rating it as biased against its own side. The article is closed access, Unpaywall records no repository copy, and it was not read for this entry, so what it did is reported here as Gunther and Schmitt, Christen and colleagues, and Reid describe it.

evidence: Gunther and Schmitt ran the study that separates the effect from the medium. They recruited 64 anti-GM foods partisans at a natural foods co-op meeting and 87 pro-GM partisans at a biotechnology conference, plus 86 neutral controls, and gave them one text on genetically modified foods in two dressings. Half read it as a newspaper story clipped from USA Today, half as a composition-class essay by a university senior, with three typos added to the essay. On the six-item bias index the news article split the partisans: pro-GM readers saw it as tilted against GM foods at -0.32 and anti-GM readers saw it as favouring GM foods at 1.03, t(71) = 3.74, p < .001. The essay did not split them, at 0.60 and 0.23, t(74) = 1.01, not significant, and the source by group interaction was F(1, 142) = 11.7, p < .01. Controls rated the article -0.21 and the essay 0. Adding demographic covariates left the article result at F(1, 67) = 11.39, p < .01 and the essay result at F(1, 64) = 0.19. Their second measure asked the same people about influence on themselves and on a neutral reader. In the article the content read as neutral for one's own opinion at -0.03 and disagreeable for neutral others at -0.37, t(71) = 2.99, p < .001. In the essay it read as agreeable for both, at 0.74 and 0.33, t(75) = 4.02, p < .001. Christen, Kannaovakun and Gunther took the effect off campus during the 1997 Teamsters strike against United Parcel Service. Eighty-four UPS managers, 51 Teamsters and 54 neutral students read one constructed Associated Press story. On an 11-point scale the Teamsters saw it as biased towards UPS at 1.1 and the managers saw it as biased towards the Teamsters at 1.2, with the neutrals near zero, F(2, 184) = 27.77 and F(2, 185) = 23.95, both p < .001.

replication.headline: The perception reappears across issues, media and decades, and two preregistered experiments on 1,636 Americans found it again for contested stories and not for uncontested ones.
replication.detail: Lo Iacono and Dores Cruz ran two preregistered experiments on Amazon Mechanical Turk, labelling identical short news items as CNN or Fox News. In the police study, N = 817, a one-point rise on a seven-point conservatism scale raised perceived bias by 0.15 points when a story about an officer killing a civilian carried the CNN label rather than the Fox label, s.e. = 0.04, p < 0.001. The same contrast for a story about an officer saving a life gave 0.05, s.e. = 0.06, p = 0.129. In the COVID-19 study, N = 819, the contrast gave 0.23 points for coverage of protests against distancing rules and 0.20 points for coverage of compliance, both s.e. = 0.05, p < 0.001. Sharing intentions barely moved, which is the authors' own headline. Hansen and Kim pooled 34 studies of the effect. Their abstract, read through OpenAlex, reports that it appears in diverse contexts at a moderate size, that involvement raises it, that it is still present at low involvement, and that neither media format nor experimental versus survey design moderates it. Older work converges from other directions. Giner-Sorolla and Chaiken's abstract reports Mideast partisans judging coverage as biased against their own side and abortion partisans showing a much less consistent pattern. Gunther, Christen, Liebhart and Chia's field experiment on primate research found partisans judging news articles as biased in a disagreeable direction relative to the other side, and that perceived slant then shaped their estimates of public opinion. Reid's third experiment, N = 119 after exclusions, gave a source effect on perceived bias of F(1, 115) = 56.24, p < .001, partial eta squared = .33, qualified by the reader's political position, F = 14.64, p < .001, partial eta squared = .11.

study.cite: Lo Iacono, S., & Dores Cruz, T. D. (2022). Hostile media perception affects news bias, but not news sharing intentions. Royal Society Open Science, 9(4), 211504.

limits: The pooled number everybody quotes was not obtained. Hansen and Kim's article is behind Taylor and Francis, which returns 403, Unpaywall reports no open copy and Semantic Scholar marks it closed, and the publisher abstract carried by Crossref and OpenAlex gives no figure. A correlation of .30 circulates in search-engine summaries of that paper and it is not published here, because a snippet is not a source. The original 1985 article was not read either, for the same reason. The conditions under which the effect fails are well mapped. Gunther and Schmitt's essay condition killed it, and Lo Iacono's positive police story killed it, so the content has to be one the sides are already fighting over. Gunther, Miller and Liebhart recruited 152 partisans on genetically modified wild rice, varied apparent circulation and source, and report that reach moved bias judgements in the predicted direction while overall evaluations tended towards assimilation rather than contrast. Gunther and Liebhart, testing journalist against student and mass circulation against classroom, found support for a categorisation bias and not for the other mechanisms proposed. Involvement is doing heavy lifting. Christen and colleagues found no reliable link between attitudes and perceived bias among their 122 students. Among the students who did identify with a side the direction ran the other way. Pro-Teamster students saw the article as favourable to the Teamsters at 0.67, and pro-UPS students saw it as favourable to UPS at 0.94. The measure itself is unstable. Litovsky asked 102 MTurk workers about one New York Times article on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and got a bias rating of 3.13 when they judged eight specific passages against 4.56 when they judged the piece as a whole, t(100) = 3.9, p < .001. Lo Iacono's design also swaps the outlet label rather than holding one neutral source, so it measures a difference in slopes across outlets, which is the relative form of the claim. Their text gives a standard error of 0.06 for the null police result where their table gives 0.041.
misreadings: The commonest error is treating a relative result as an absolute one. Gunther and Schmitt's own table separates them item by item on one dataset. On perceived bias in the portrayal of GM foods supporters, both partisan groups saw the article slanted the same way and the anti-GM readers saw more of it, which is the relative effect. On the percentage of favourable content and on the author's own bias, the two groups landed on opposite sides, which is the absolute effect. A paper reporting that partisans differed has not shown that either side saw hostility. The second error is folding this into the third-person effect. That effect compares perceived influence on oneself against perceived influence on others, and this one compares readings of content. Gunther and Schmitt connect them by mechanism rather than by measure, arguing that partisans see hostility once they picture a broad audience receiving the piece. The third error is inferring that the coverage was fair. Establishing a stimulus as neutral takes separate work, and Gunther and Schmitt did it with nine pretest judges and 86 nonpartisan readers whose mean bias rating was -0.21. The fourth error is expecting the perception to drive behaviour. Christen and colleagues found partisans' estimates of public opinion tracking their own views rather than the bias they had just reported, with personal opinion correlating .42 with perceived public support and -.41 with perceived opposition. Lo Iacono and Dores Cruz found the perception left sharing intentions on social media roughly where they were. Naive realism is offered as the account of why the effect happens, and it is a framework rather than a rival finding.
